title: THEY MEANT TO DESTROY YOU. GOD WAS NOT FINISHED WRITING YOUR STORY.
paragraphs: THEY MEANT TO DESTROY YOU. GOD WAS NOT FINISHED WRITING YOUR STORY.
If God Is Good, Why Did He Allow What They Did to You? The Disturbing Truth Behind Genesis 50:20 and Acts 2:23 That Leads From Betrayal to the Cross.
What if the worst thing someone ever did to you was not the final chapter of your story?

What if the betrayal that shattered your trust, the injustice that stole your peace, the rejection that made you question your worth, and the suffering that brought you to your knees were not beyond God's power to redeem?
But before you answer, there is something we need to confront.
Something uncomfortable.
Something that has caused believers to wrestle with God through sleepless nights, unanswered prayers, and tears nobody else ever saw.
Can God use an evil action to accomplish His good purposes without ever approving of the evil itself?
Because if He can, that changes how we understand suffering.
And if we misunderstand that truth, we may end up blaming God for the very wickedness He condemns.
Somewhere, someone is reading this while carrying a wound that still has a name.
A father who abandoned them.
A spouse who betrayed them.
A friend who exposed their secrets.
A leader who abused their trust.
A person who smiled in their face while quietly working against them.
And perhaps the most painful part was not simply what happened.
It was what happened afterward.
You prayed.
You waited.
You wondered why God did not stop it.
You watched people who hurt you continue with their lives while you struggled to put yours back together.
And somewhere in the silence, a question began forming that you were almost afraid to ask:
Lord, if You knew what they were going to do, why did You allow it?
The Bible does not mock that question.
It does not demand that wounded people pretend evil was good.
And it does not offer the shallow comfort of telling every suffering person that everything happened because God wanted them to be hurt.
Instead, Scripture takes us into two of the darkest scenes in human history.
One involves a young man betrayed by his own brothers.
The other involves the Son of God betrayed, condemned, and crucified.
And in both stories, we discover a truth so astonishing that it forces us to reconsider what evil can accomplish when it encounters the sovereign purposes of God.
Human beings can intend evil. God can accomplish good through the very event they intended for evil. And their evil remains evil.
That distinction matters more than most people realize.
Joseph knew what betrayal felt like long before he understood what God would do through it.
He was seventeen when his brothers' jealousy turned into hatred.
They resented their father's favoritism. They hated Joseph's dreams. They could not stand the thought that the younger brother might one day stand above them.
And when an opportunity came, they acted.
They stripped him of his special robe.
They threw him into a pit.
Then, instead of rescuing him, they sold him into slavery.
Imagine the scene.
Joseph looking upward from the pit.
The faces of his brothers disappearing above him.
The sound of their voices continuing while his future collapsed.
Genesis 42:21 later reveals that Joseph had pleaded with them in anguish, but they refused to listen.
He begged.
They heard him.
And they did it anyway.
That detail matters.
Because some wounds are not caused by misunderstanding.
Sometimes people know they are hurting you.
Sometimes they see the tears.
Sometimes they hear the pleading.
And they still choose to continue.
Joseph was carried away from his home into Egypt, separated from his father and everything familiar.
And his suffering did not end there.
He served in Potiphar's household, resisted the sexual advances of Potiphar's wife, and was falsely accused after refusing her.
His integrity did not protect him from imprisonment.
His obedience did not produce immediate deliverance.
He did what was right and still suffered for it.
Think about that.
There are people who believe that if they obey God faithfully enough, they will never experience injustice.
Joseph's life destroys that illusion.
Sometimes faithfulness leads you through a prison before you ever see the palace.
Sometimes doing the right thing costs you something precious.
Sometimes you can be exactly where obedience has led you and still find yourself surrounded by circumstances you never would have chosen.
Yet Genesis repeatedly tells us something remarkable.
The LORD was with Joseph.
Not merely when he became powerful.
Not merely when his circumstances improved.
God was with him in the house where he served and in the prison where he suffered.
The presence of God was not proved by the absence of hardship.
And Joseph's imprisonment was not evidence that God had abandoned him.
Years passed.
Joseph eventually interpreted Pharaoh's dreams, was elevated to authority in Egypt, and administered preparations that preserved food through a devastating famine.
The same brothers who sold him eventually stood before him, desperate for grain.
They did not recognize him.
But Joseph recognized them.
Imagine that moment.
The people who once controlled his suffering were now standing before a man who possessed the power to punish them.
He could have used his authority to destroy them.
He could have made them experience the helplessness he once experienced.
Instead, after testing their character and seeing evidence of change, Joseph eventually revealed himself.
And later, after their father's death, the brothers feared that Joseph would finally take revenge.
That is when Joseph spoke words that have echoed through generations.
Genesis 50:20, in the King James Version, declares:
"But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive."
Read that carefully.
Joseph did not say, "What you did was not evil."
He did not say, "You were secretly doing the right thing."
He did not excuse their cruelty or pretend the betrayal never happened.
He named their intention.
Evil.
Then he revealed something about God's purpose.
Good.
The original Hebrew makes the contrast especially striking.
אַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה וֵאלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
Attem chashavtem alai ra'ah, ve'Elohim chashavah letovah.
A close rendering is:
"You planned evil against me, but God planned it for good."
The Hebrew verb chashav (חָשַׁב) appears in both clauses. In this context, it carries the sense of planning, devising, or intending.
Joseph's brothers planned evil.
God planned good.
The same historical event stood within two radically different intentions.
Their purpose was betrayal and removal.
God's purpose was preservation of life.
And here is the extraordinary part.
God did not need to approve of their wicked motives in order to accomplish His righteous purpose.
Their hatred belonged to them.
Their guilt belonged to them.
God's wisdom and goodness belonged to Him.

The text does not portray God as the author of their moral evil. Nor does it portray Him as helplessly improvising after their sin. It presents a sovereign God accomplishing a good purpose through events in which human beings were genuinely responsible for their wicked choices.
That does not answer every philosophical question about divine sovereignty and human freedom.
Faithful Christians have debated those questions for centuries.
But it establishes something the text refuses to let us ignore.
God's sovereignty does not make evil morally good.
And human wickedness does not place events beyond God's power.
Now consider something else.
Joseph could see a particular purpose because God had brought him to a place where that purpose became visible.
He saw that many lives had been preserved during the famine.
But Scripture does not promise that every believer will discover a similarly identifiable explanation for every tragedy.
Some suffering remains mysterious in this life.
Some losses are not reversed.
Some relationships are not restored.
Some people die without seeing earthly justice.
We must never use Joseph's story to promise that every victim will become wealthy, powerful, publicly vindicated, or reunited with those who hurt them.
That is not the Gospel.
And we must never tell an abused person to remain in danger because God might use their suffering.
God's ability to redeem evil does not excuse the person committing it.
Forgiveness does not require denying what happened.
Reconciliation requires more than words; where serious harm has occurred, safety, truth, accountability, and genuine repentance matter.
Joseph's story gives us hope without requiring us to pretend that pain is harmless.
But there is another story.
One that goes deeper.
One that takes us beyond a pit in Canaan and a prison in Egypt.
It takes us to a hill outside Jerusalem.
And there, the question becomes almost unbearable.
If God can use evil without approving of evil, what do we do with the crucifixion of Jesus Christ?
Because the cross was not merely a tragedy.
It was an injustice of staggering proportions.
Jesus Christ was sinless.
He healed the sick.
He welcomed sinners to repentance.
He showed mercy to the broken.
He exposed religious hypocrisy.
He spoke the truth about the Father.
Yet He was betrayed, falsely accused, mocked, beaten, and handed over for execution.
The religious authorities who opposed Him were accountable for their actions.
Judas was accountable for his betrayal.
The Roman authorities and soldiers were accountable for their injustice and cruelty.
And still, when the apostle Peter stood before the crowd at Pentecost, he declared something that should make every reader stop.
Acts 2:23, in the King James Version, says:
"Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain."
Notice the two truths standing together.
Jesus was delivered according to God's determined purpose and foreknowledge.
And the people who crucified Him acted wickedly.
Peter did not erase human guilt because God's purpose was being fulfilled.
He did not suggest that crucifixion became righteous simply because salvation would come through it.
He proclaimed divine sovereignty and human responsibility in the same breath.
The Greek text begins with a remarkable expression:
τοῦτον τῇ ὡρισμένῃ βουλῇ καὶ προγνώσει τοῦ θεοῦ ἔκδοτον
Touton tē hōrismenē boulē kai prognōsei tou theou ekdoton.
A close translation is:
"This one, handed over by the determined plan and foreknowledge of God."
The word boulē (βουλή) refers here to counsel, purpose, or plan.
The participle hōrismenē (ὡρισμένῃ) communicates something determined or appointed.
And prognōsis (πρόγνωσις) means foreknowledge.
Peter is not describing a God who was surprised by the cross.
The crucifixion was not an emergency that forced heaven to invent a rescue plan.
Yet the same verse attributes the killing of Jesus to lawless human action.
The cross was within God's redemptive purpose.
The crucifiers were still guilty of their sin.
And Acts 4:27–28 reinforces this truth when the early believers pray about the opposition of Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel against Jesus.
Their prayer acknowledges that these opponents acted in ways encompassed by God's predetermined purpose.
The Bible does not explain away their responsibility.
It holds both truths together.
Now we reach the heart of the matter.
God did not call the murder of His Son good. God accomplished the greatest good through the greatest injustice ever committed.
The distinction is everything.
The betrayal was evil.
The false accusations were evil.
The mockery was evil.
The cruelty was evil.
The unjust condemnation was evil.
But the saving purpose of God was holy.
Jesus was not merely a helpless victim caught in circumstances beyond divine control.
He willingly gave His life.
In John 10:18, Jesus explains that no one takes His life from Him in the ultimate sense; He lays it down of His own accord.
And in the garden of Gethsemane, He submitted Himself to the Father's will.
This was not the Father approving human cruelty.
This was the Son willingly entering human suffering to accomplish redemption.
The crucifixion reveals both the wickedness of human sin and the immeasurable love of God.
At the cross, justice was not dismissed as unimportant.
Sin was not redefined as harmless.
Rather, Christ bore our sins, fulfilling the saving purpose described in passages such as Isaiah 53, Romans 3:25–26, and 1 Peter 2:24.
And on the third day, He rose from the dead.
Death did not have the final word.
The tomb did not have the final word.
The wicked intentions of those who condemned Him did not have the final word.
Jesus Christ rose victorious.
That is why the cross cannot be reduced to a motivational slogan about turning bad days into good ones.
The Gospel is far greater than that.
It announces that sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and given new life through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And here is where this truth becomes deeply personal.
Because perhaps you have spent years believing that what happened to you has permanently disqualified you from being loved, useful, or restored.
Maybe you have replayed the betrayal so many times that it has become part of how you see yourself.
You no longer say, "Someone betrayed me."
You say, "I am someone nobody stays for."
You no longer say, "I experienced injustice."
You say, "My life is ruined."
You no longer say, "I made a terrible mistake."
You say, "I am beyond forgiveness."
But the Gospel confronts those conclusions.
Your suffering may have shaped parts of your story.
It does not have the authority to determine your ultimate worth before God.
And your sin, however serious, need not be the final word if you turn to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
There is a difference between acknowledging what happened and allowing it to become your identity.
There is a difference between remembering your wounds and believing that your wounds are all you are.
And there is a difference between trusting God's power to redeem and pretending that every terrible event was secretly wonderful.
God does not ask you to celebrate evil.
He calls you to trust Him in a world where evil is real, justice matters, and redemption is possible.
Perhaps you are still in the part of the story that feels like Joseph's prison.
You have not seen the outcome.
You cannot explain the delay.
You are trying to remain faithful while everything around you feels uncertain.
Then hear this carefully.
You do not need to invent a beautiful explanation for your suffering to be loved by God.
You do not need to call your trauma a blessing.
You do not need to smile while your heart is breaking.
The Psalms contain cries of anguish.
Job wrestled with devastating loss.
Jeremiah lamented.
Even Jesus wept.
Biblical faith is not emotional dishonesty.
It is bringing the truth of our pain before the God who sees.
And when you cannot trace His purposes, you can still look to the character of God revealed in Jesus Christ.
The cross tells us that God is not indifferent to suffering.
The resurrection tells us that suffering and death will not ultimately defeat His saving purpose.
But there is a warning here too.
God's ability to bring good from evil must never become permission for us to do evil.
Romans 3:8 explicitly rejects the reasoning that we should do evil so that good may result.
James 1:13 teaches that God does not tempt anyone with evil.
And James 1:17 describes God as the giver of good gifts.
We cannot defend our cruelty by saying God will use it.
We cannot excuse dishonesty because someone might learn from it.
We cannot justify abuse because a victim might eventually grow stronger.
The possibility of redemption does not erase moral responsibility.
If you are the person who caused the wound, Joseph's story is not your permission slip.
It is your invitation to repent.
Stop hiding behind God's sovereignty.
Confess what you did.
Turn away from the sin.
Make restitution where possible.
Accept accountability.
Seek forgiveness without demanding it.
And understand that another person's healing does not automatically cancel your responsibility for the harm you caused.
Grace does not require pretending that justice is unnecessary.
True repentance bears fruit.
But perhaps the evil you are struggling with today is not something another person did.
Perhaps it is something you did.
A decision you regret.
A betrayal you committed.
A lie you told.
A relationship you destroyed.
A season of rebellion you cannot undo.
And you wonder whether God could possibly receive you after everything.
Then remember who stood at the cross.
There was a criminal dying beside Jesus.
He could not travel backward in time.
He could not erase his crimes.
He could not rebuild his reputation.
He could only turn toward the Savior and ask to be remembered.
And Jesus gave him a promise of paradise (Luke 23:39–43).
That man was not saved because his past suddenly became righteous.
He was saved by the mercy of Christ.
That is grace.
Not permission to continue in sin.
Not denial of guilt.
Not an excuse to avoid repentance.
Grace is God's undeserved favor toward sinners through Jesus Christ, a mercy that forgives and begins to transform those who come to Him.
This is why our message is not simply that God can turn your pain into a platform.
Our message is that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
He restores people who could never restore themselves.
He gives hope to the ashamed.
He calls the wandering home.
He gives new life to those who trust Him.
And He is able to sustain His people even when the explanation for their suffering remains hidden.
Not because every scandal ends in public success.
Not because every wound disappears.
Not because every person who betrayed you returns with an apology.
But because the risen Christ has the authority to redeem sinners, sustain the suffering, and bring His people into a future that evil cannot finally destroy.
Romans 8:28 promises that God works all things together for good for those who love Him and are called according to His purpose.
And the following verse helps us understand that good.
Romans 8:29 speaks of being conformed to the image of God's Son.
God's ultimate purpose is not merely our comfort, prosperity, or public vindication.
It is our conformity to Christ and our final redemption in Him.
That matters when life does not improve according to our preferred schedule.
Because God's faithfulness cannot be measured only by how quickly circumstances change.
Sometimes His sustaining grace is seen in the strength to endure another day.
Sometimes it is seen in the courage to tell the truth.
Sometimes it is seen in repentance after years of running.
Sometimes it is seen in the willingness to seek help, establish boundaries, or walk away from danger.
Sometimes it is seen in forgiveness that grows slowly, without denying the need for justice.
And sometimes it is seen in a wounded believer whispering a prayer when there are no words left for anything else.
You may not know what God will do with every broken piece of your life.
Joseph did not know while he was in the pit.
He did not know while he was being sold.
He did not know while he was imprisoned.
But we know something Joseph's story points us toward and the resurrection of Jesus confirms.
Evil is not sovereign.
God is.
And the God who raised Jesus from the dead has not surrendered His purposes to the darkness of this world.
That does not mean every outcome will make sense today.
It means our hope rests in someone greater than our ability to understand.
So perhaps the question you need to ask tonight is not simply, "Why did God allow this?"
Perhaps another question belongs beside it.
"Lord, how do I remain faithful to You while I am still hurting?"
"How do I seek justice without surrendering my heart to hatred?"
"How do I forgive without pretending the wrong was acceptable?"
"How do I repent of my own sins without believing I am beyond Your mercy?"
"How do I trust You when I cannot see what You are doing?"
These are not questions for people who have mastered faith.
They are questions for people who desperately need Jesus.
And that is precisely where the Gospel meets us.
Not at the moment we become impressive.
Not when we finally learn to hide our weakness.
Not when we have a perfect testimony with a beautiful ending.
But when we come honestly before the Savior and acknowledge our need for Him.
Maybe that is you.
Maybe you have been attending church while quietly losing hope.
Maybe you have been encouraging everybody else while struggling to pray for yourself.
Maybe you have been posting Scripture while privately wrestling with resentment.
Maybe you have been calling yourself a Christian while resisting the repentance Christ has been calling you toward.
Or maybe you have never truly surrendered your life to Jesus at all.
Wherever you are, the invitation is not to manufacture a dramatic spiritual experience.
It is to come to Christ in truth.
Confess your sin.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Turn toward Him.
Receive the mercy that you could never earn.
And begin walking in obedience, supported by His grace.
If you need words for that surrender, you can pray:

"Lord Jesus, I confess that I need Your mercy. I have sinned against You, and I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me, change my heart, and teach me to follow You. Where I have been wounded, help me seek healing without embracing bitterness. Where I have done wrong, give me the courage to repent and make things right. Teach me to trust Your goodness even when I do not understand my circumstances. My hope is in You alone. Amen."
A prayer is not a formula that saves by its wording.
Salvation is by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by the performance of a religious ritual (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But if that prayer expresses the genuine turning of your heart toward Him, do not dismiss the importance of that moment.
And do not walk alone.
Find a faithful, Bible-teaching local church where you can grow, be discipled, and learn to follow Christ alongside other believers.
Because following Jesus is not meant to be a lonely performance.
It is a life of grace, truth, repentance, love, and growing obedience.
And perhaps this is where you can help someone else.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who has quietly concluded that their life is too broken for God to use.
Someone is carrying shame over a past they cannot change.
Someone has been betrayed and is beginning to believe that God must have abandoned them.
Someone has confused God's sovereignty with God's approval of evil.
Someone desperately needs to hear that the cross was not heaven's defeat and that resurrection is real.
Not merely to increase the reach of a page.
You may never know who reads it in the middle of a sleepless night.
You may never know who needed that reminder to seek help, return to prayer, repent of sin, or open the Bible again.

And if someone came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them with kindness and sensitivity. If their struggle is private, send the article directly instead of exposing their pain in a public comment.
Do not make their suffering a spectacle.
Make your encouragement personal.
You can simply write "Christ is still healing me" if you are learning to trust Him through wounds that have not fully healed.
Write "I'm still fighting" if you are weary but determined to keep following Jesus.
Or write "Jesus, forgive me" if the Holy Spirit has brought you face to face with something you need to confess and turn away from.
You do not owe strangers the details of your suffering. You can share only what is safe and appropriate.
But your honest testimony may help another person realize that they are not the only one wrestling with faith in the middle of pain.
And invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, those who have drifted from their faith, and even people who do not yet know Jesus to follow along.
We are not building a community around the illusion that Christians never suffer.
We want to build a community that keeps pointing suffering people, repentant sinners, and searching hearts toward the risen Christ.
That is also why we are committed to making biblical resources accessible.
These resources are offered to encourage serious study, spiritual maturity, and continued growth in the Gospel.
And if this ministry has strengthened your faith, there is another meaningful way you can help us continue.
For those who choose to make this part of their regular Christian giving, it can be an expression of generosity toward ministry work.
But we want to be clear about something important.
Scripture calls believers to give willingly and cheerfully, not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7). Christians also have responsibilities toward their local churches, families, and people in need.
We would never want anyone to neglect those responsibilities or give beyond their means because they feel spiritually pressured.
For those who can, it is a practical way to help us continue producing and sharing Christ-centered teaching, strengthening discipleship resources, and reaching more people with the message of Jesus.
These products are not the reason we proclaim the Gospel.
They are simply another way to encourage believers, share biblical messages, and express our appreciation to those who help sustain the ministry.
It is about Jesus Christ.
His Word.
His Gospel.
His grace toward sinners.
His power to transform lives.
And His promise to complete the good work He has begun in His people (Philippians 1:6).
Before you leave, I want you to return to the question that brought us here.
Can God use evil actions to accomplish His purposes without approving of evil?
Joseph's testimony says yes.
Peter's preaching at Pentecost says yes.
The cross of Jesus Christ gives us the clearest and greatest demonstration.
But that truth should never make us careless about evil.

It should make us more serious about holiness, more courageous in seeking justice, more compassionate toward the wounded, more humble about what we do not understand, and more grateful for the grace that comes through Christ.
The brothers meant evil.
God accomplished good.
The crucifiers acted wickedly.
God accomplished redemption through the willing sacrifice of His Son.
And the risen Jesus now calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
That is where our confidence belongs.
Not in the promise that every betrayal will make us successful.
Not in the assumption that every tragedy will be explained before we die.
Not in the fantasy that faithful Christians never suffer.
But in the crucified and risen Savior who has overcome sin and death.
So if you are still in the pit, do not mistake the darkness for proof that God has disappeared.
If you are still in the prison, do not assume that your suffering makes your obedience meaningless.
If you are struggling with guilt, do not use God's sovereignty to excuse your sin.
And if you are longing for forgiveness, do not imagine that your past is stronger than the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Bring your pain into the light.
Bring your sin into the light.
Bring your unanswered questions to the Lord.
And remember that the One who suffered unjustly, died for sinners, and rose victorious is worthy of your trust.
Because the greatest hope of the Christian faith is not that God will make every chapter of our earthly lives pleasant.
It is that Jesus Christ has opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God, and that those who belong to Him have a living hope that even death cannot extinguish.
And when the final chapter is written, the victory will belong to Him.
The hands that nailed Jesus to the cross could not stop the hands that would rise from the grave—and the evil that wounded your story will never have the authority to rewrite His Gospel.
